title: Guest basket is cleared after partial merge failure
description: The basket merge workflow is expected to continue after an existing basket item's PUT fails, then clear the guest basket and report completion. The guest basket contains three units of Product 1 and three units of Product 2 (lines 201-204); the update of the existing Product 1 basket item fails with HTTP 500 (lines 221-224), but the test still expects the merge to complete and the guest basket to be deleted (lines 231-232). This creates a non-atomic merge: a transient failure can permanently discard guest-basket contents that were not successfully merged, causing data loss and an integrity violation. The production caller of the service is outside this file.

trace.description: The service merge operation is invoked for basket 42; the production caller of this service is outside this file.
The guest basket contains duplicate Product 1 entries and Product 2 quantities that must be merged into the authenticated user's basket.
The service locates the server-side basket and an existing Product 1 basket item before attempting the merge.
The update request for existing BasketItem 100 fails with HTTP 500, leaving part of the merge incomplete.

Despite the failed update, the test expects a subsequent POST for another item and then expects the operation to complete and guestBasket to be removed. Clearing the source state without successful completion can permanently lose the unmerged Product 1 quantity.

title: Unbounded chat request and streamed-response consumption
description: `streamMessages` accepts an unrestricted messages array and forwards it directly in an HTTP request without enforcing message-count, content-length, or request-size limits. The same method also accumulates every streamed response chunk in an in-memory array. A caller capable of invoking this service can submit very large conversations, causing excessive request bandwidth, server-side model/token consumption, and browser memory usage; a large or runaway streamed response can further grow `chunks` without an application-level cap. No rate limit or size/turn bound is visible in this client-side control path.

trace.description: `streamMessages` receives the caller-supplied `messages` array; the caller is outside this file, and no upper bound is enforced on the number or size of messages.
The unrestricted messages array is serialized directly into a POST request to the chat endpoint, with no client-side request-size, timeout, or rate control shown.
Each parsed streamed response chunk is appended to the unbounded `chunks` array, and there is no maximum response size, chunk count, or generation limit enforced in this service.

title: Private key transmitted to REST API
description: The service contract sends a caller-provided blockchain private key directly to the REST API in the request body. A private key should remain client-side and be used for local signing; transmitting it to a backend gives that backend, and any intermediary or compromised endpoint, control over the wallet. The test also targets an explicit HTTP URL, although this file uses a mocked HTTP client and therefore does not prove the production transport configuration.

trace.description: The service receives a private-key value from its caller; the real caller is outside this test file, while the test supplies the representative value.
The value is propagated into a POST request to the web3 submission endpoint using an explicit HTTP URL.
The request body contains the private key in plaintext as the `privateKey` field, exposing wallet-signing material to the API rather than keeping it local for signing.

title: Basket operations accept arbitrary resource identifiers without ownership enforcement
description: The service accepts caller-supplied basket or basket-item identifiers and directly places them into API requests without any ownership or authorization check. A caller outside this file can invoke `find`, `get`, `put`, `del`, `checkout`, or `applyCoupon` with another user's basket/item ID. If the corresponding API endpoint does not independently enforce ownership, User A can substitute User B's identifier to read, modify, delete, apply coupons to, or check out User B's basket.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the basket identifier to the exported `find` method; the method does not establish that the identifier belongs to the authenticated user.
The supplied identifier is interpolated directly into the basket lookup request and the response is returned to the caller, with no per-resource ownership check in this service.

title: Unrestricted basket payload forwarding enables mass-assignment if the API auto-binds fields
description: The exported update and create wrappers accept `params` as `any` and forward the entire caller-provided object to the basket API. There is no explicit property allow-list in this service. If the backend binds request fields directly to a basket or basket-item model, callers may set fields they should not control, such as ownership, product, pricing, or workflow-related properties. Server-side property authorization is required; this client wrapper provides none.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies an untyped `params` object to the exported `put` method; no permitted-field schema is applied.
The complete caller-controlled object is forwarded as the PUT request body to the basket-item API, without an explicit property allow-list.

title: Unencoded coupon input permits URL path injection
description: The coupon value is caller-controlled and is interpolated into a URL path without URL encoding or an allow-list. Delimiters such as `/`, `?`, `#`, or encoded path characters can alter the request path or query interpretation, potentially causing route confusion or reaching a different server-side operation than intended. Coupon values should be encoded as a path segment or sent as a validated request body field.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the coupon string to the exported `applyCoupon` method.
The untrusted coupon is concatenated directly into the request URL path and sent through `HttpClient` without `encodeURIComponent` or an equivalent strict allow-list.

title: Unvalidated guest-basket quantities are forwarded during basket merge
description: Guest-basket quantities are accepted from the caller without enforcing a positive, finite, bounded value. In particular, `addToGuestBasket` adds the caller-supplied `quantity` directly to an existing item or stores it as a new item. A caller can supply a negative quantity, causing the local basket to contain a negative line quantity. During merge, that value is added to the server-side basket quantity or submitted as a new `BasketItem` quantity, potentially reducing the basket quantity or manipulating the final order total if the backend does not independently reject it. Positive quantities are also unbounded, allowing excessively large values to be persisted and forwarded.

trace.description: Entrypoint: `addToGuestBasket(productId, quantity)` receives the product identifier and quantity from a caller outside this file.
The caller-supplied quantity is added directly to an existing guest item without a positivity, finiteness, or upper-bound check.
For a new product, the same unchecked quantity is stored in sessionStorage as basket state.

When the guest basket is merged, the unchecked quantity is combined with the server basket quantity and sent in a PUT request, or sent directly in a new basket-item save request. This is the security-relevant sink because attacker-controlled negative or excessively large quantities cross into persisted server-side basket data.

title: Unbounded local backup size enables client-side resource exhaustion
description: The restore workflow accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied File and reads its entire contents into memory before parsing it, with no file-size limit or parsing budget. A user who can induce a victim to select a very large backup file can cause substantial memory allocation and CPU consumption in the browser through `backupFile.text()` and `JSON.parse`, potentially freezing or crashing the client. The caller is outside this file, but the exported `restore` method provides the unbounded input boundary.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies an attacker-influenced `File` object to the exported `restore` method.
The complete file is read into memory with `backupFile.text()`; there is no size check before the read.
The complete attacker-controlled text is synchronously deserialized with `JSON.parse`, causing memory allocation and CPU use proportional to the unbounded file size.

title: Untrusted feedback comment marked as trusted HTML
description: Feedback comments received from the external feedback service are interpolated directly into an HTML fragment and then explicitly marked as trusted with DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(). This disables Angular's normal HTML sanitization. An attacker who can submit or otherwise influence a feedback comment can inject HTML, including executable event-handler payloads such as an onerror attribute, which will execute when the trusted value is rendered by the component template.

trace.description: The component receives feedback records from feedbackService.find(); the caller and external data source are outside this file.
Each feedback comment is interpolated into a raw HTML string without validation or context-appropriate sanitization. The comment value is attacker-influenced if a user can submit feedback.

The constructed HTML containing the untrusted comment is passed to bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), explicitly disabling Angular's built-in sanitization before the value is rendered. This creates a client-side HTML injection/XSS sink.

title: Stored client-side XSS through trusted feedback comment HTML
description:
Feedback comments returned by the external feedback service are embedded directly into an HTML fragment and then explicitly marked as trusted with Angular's sanitization bypass. An attacker who can submit or influence a feedback comment can break out of the intended

element and inject executable HTML, such as event-handler attributes or other active elements, when the gallery renders the trusted value. No sanitization or allowlisting is applied before the bypass.

trace.description: The component receives the feedbacks collection from feedbackService.find().subscribe(); the caller and the external feedback data source are outside this file.

Each feedback comment is interpolated into an HTML fragment inside a

element without encoding or validation, while the rating is also incorporated into the fragment.
The constructed HTML is passed as gallery image arguments, providing the downstream rendering path for the feedback content.

The dynamically constructed comment HTML is explicitly passed to bypassSecurityTrustHtml(), disabling Angular's normal HTML sanitization. Attacker-controlled markup can therefore be interpreted as HTML by the gallery's rendering context, enabling client-side HTML/script-context injection such as event-handler XSS.

title: Raw backend errors are exposed through browser-console logging
description: The tests explicitly verify that raw API error values are written directly to the browser console. In particular, the price-modification failure passes an error object through the component and expects that object to be logged unchanged. If the real backend error contains stack traces, internal identifiers, or other diagnostic details, any user able to access the browser can inspect them through developer tools. The implementation of modifyPrice is outside this file, so the exact production contents of the error are not confirmable here.

trace.description: The test invokes the component's price-modification workflow; its external caller is outside this file.
The mocked service rejects with an error object, modeling an API response that is propagated to the component's error handler.
The test verifies that the raw error object is sent to console.log without sanitization or restriction, establishing browser-console exposure of the error payload.

title: Password-change credentials are transmitted in a GET URL
description: The password-change contract uses an HTTP GET request with the current password, new password, and repeated password embedded directly in the query string. Query-string credentials can be captured by browser history, reverse proxies, web-server access logs, monitoring systems, and intermediary tooling, even when the transport itself uses HTTPS. An attacker who obtains such URL history or logs can recover password material and potentially compromise the account. The test explicitly locks in this unsafe method and URL shape rather than requiring a POST body or equivalent protected credential transport.

trace.description: The service's password-change operation is invoked with current, new, and repeated password values; production callers supplying these values are outside this test file.
The test expects all three password values to be placed directly into the request URL as query parameters.
The expected request method is GET, confirming that password material is transported in the URL rather than in a request body or another non-URL channel.

title: OAuth access token transmitted in URL query string
description: The test verifies that `oauthLogin` sends the OAuth access token directly in the request URL as the `access_token` query parameter. Bearer tokens in URLs can be recorded by browser history, reverse-proxy/web-server logs, monitoring systems, and potentially leaked through referrer handling, enabling token replay by anyone who obtains those records. The implementation should use an authorization header or another channel that avoids placing the credential in the URL.

trace.description: The service receives an OAuth access token from its caller; the caller and attacker-facing entrypoint are outside this test file. The test invokes `oauthLogin` with the token value `at`.
The expected outgoing request URL embeds the supplied token in the `access_token` query parameter.
The HTTP test request is matched against the token-bearing URL, establishing that the service's outgoing request places the bearer credential in URL query data rather than an authorization header.

title: Client-controlled address ID is used for update without visible ownership enforcement
description: The component accepts an attacker-controllable `addressId` from the client-side route and directly uses it to load and later update an address. There is no ownership or authorization check in this component between receiving the identifier, loading the address, and submitting the update. If the backing service/API does not independently enforce that the address belongs to the authenticated user, User A can replace the route identifier with User B's address ID and modify User B's address.

trace.description: The caller and router navigation are outside this file; the component receives the attacker-controlled `addressId` through the activated route parameter map.
The route value is copied directly into `this.addressId` and the component switches into edit mode without checking whether the current user owns or may edit the referenced address.
The component uses the unverified identifier to fetch the address via `addressService.getById`, with no visible per-resource authorization check in this code path.

When saving, the same unverified identifier is passed to `addressService.put`, creating the unauthorized-update sink if the backend does not perform its own ownership check. A proof of concept is to authenticate as User A, navigate to an edit route containing User B's address ID, change a field, and submit the form.

title: Unbounded bulk loading of inventory, products, and order history
description: Component initialization triggers several bulk retrievals without request-side pagination or an explicit result limit: stock via `quantityService.getAll()`, products via `search('')`, and orders via `orderHistoryService.getAll()`. The Angular paginators are attached only after the complete responses have been received and materialized locally, so they do not limit server response size, network usage, or client memory consumption. An attacker or ordinary user who can trigger this component can repeatedly cause potentially large datasets to be transferred and retained in browser memory; the impact depends on whether the backing services impose independent limits.

trace.description: `ngAfterViewInit` is the component lifecycle entrypoint; the framework invokes it from outside this file when the accounting view is initialized.
Initialization immediately invokes `loadQuantity`, `loadProducts`, and `loadOrders` without supplying page, limit, or range parameters.
`loadQuantity` calls `quantityService.getAll()`, requesting the complete stock collection with no visible pagination or limit.
`loadProducts` calls `productService.search('')` with an empty search term, requesting the complete matching product set rather than a bounded page.
The complete product response is assigned to `tableData` and used to construct a local `MatTableDataSource`; the paginator is attached only after all records have already been received and stored.
`loadOrders` calls `orderHistoryService.getAll()`, likewise requesting all order-history records without a visible server-side page or limit.

Every returned order is copied into `orderData` and the full array is materialized in a local `MatTableDataSource` before `paginatorOrderHistory` is attached, making the paginator client-side rather than a response-size control.

title: Inventory quantity update has no upper-bound business validation
description: `modifyQuantity` accepts an arbitrary quantity value from its caller and sends it to the quantity update operation after enforcing only a lower bound. Values of any size, including extremely large positive quantities, are accepted and transmitted. If the backend does not independently enforce a business maximum and authorization, a caller can inflate inventory quantities and corrupt stock/accounting data. The client-side check is not a security boundary because the method and its request can be invoked or reproduced outside the UI.

trace.description: `modifyQuantity(id, value)` receives the product identifier and requested quantity from a caller outside this file, such as the component template or another client-side event path.

The only validation is `value < 0 ? 0 : value`; all nonnegative values, including arbitrarily large quantities, are placed directly into the update request body and sent through `quantityService.put`.

title: Accounting mutation handlers lack visible authorization or resource-scope enforcement
description: The component exposes mutation handlers that accept caller-supplied resource identifiers and passes them directly to update APIs without any visible role, ownership, or resource-scope check. In particular, an invocation of `modifyQuantity` with another product's ID reaches `quantityService.put`, and `modifyPrice` similarly reaches `productService.put`. Because the caller and backend authorization are outside this file, this is a client-side authorization gap that becomes exploitable if these service endpoints do not independently enforce the accounting/admin permission and target-resource authorization; a user could substitute another product or order identifier and alter it.

trace.description: `modifyQuantity(id, value)` receives the target resource identifier from a caller outside this file.
The caller-supplied `id` is used directly in the quantity update request; only a negative-value clamp is applied to `value`, with no authorization or ownership check.
`quantityService.put` performs the target-resource mutation using the unverified identifier.

title: Accounting workflow trusts client-controlled price, quantity, and delivery-state values
description: The component forwards business-state inputs to mutation APIs with only a lower-bound check for numeric values and no visible type, finite-value, upper-bound, or state-transition validation. `changeDeliveryStatus` forwards an arbitrary `deliveryStatus` for an arbitrary order, while price and quantity updates accept arbitrary caller-provided values (including values such as NaN or non-numeric data if they reach these handlers). The UI therefore does not enforce the accounting workflow or trustworthy server-derived values; if the backend relies on this component's controls, an attacker can manipulate prices, quantities, or delivery state directly through the client.

trace.description: `changeDeliveryStatus(deliveryStatus, orderId)` accepts both the order identifier and the new delivery state from a caller outside this file.
The raw `deliveryStatus` value is placed into the update payload without an allow-list or transition/prerequisite check.
`orderHistoryService.toggleDeliveryStatus` submits the caller-selected state for the caller-selected order, making the API mutation the sink for the unvalidated business decision.

title: Unbounded address collection loaded into browser memory
description: The component retrieves the complete address collection and materializes every returned record in browser memory without a visible page size, item limit, or pagination boundary. If the backing AddressService/API returns an attacker-inflatable or otherwise large collection, a user can trigger excessive network transfer, JavaScript heap usage, and table-rendering work. The service or infrastructure may impose limits elsewhere, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The component is initialized by an Angular caller outside this file; ngOnInit unconditionally invokes load().
load() calls AddressService.get() without supplying pagination, a maximum result count, or another visible resource bound.

The returned collection is assigned directly to storedAddresses and used to construct a MatTableDataSource for the entire result set, causing all returned records to be retained and processed by the browser.

title: Full service errors exposed through browser console logging
description: The error handlers write the complete error object to the browser console. Because the object originates from the HTTP/service failure path, it can include backend response bodies, stack traces, internal URLs, or other sensitive diagnostic data. This is a low-confidence finding because the contents of the error response and whether production builds strip console logging are not visible here.

trace.description: An external caller or Angular event invokes deleteAddress with an address identifier; the caller is outside this file.
The identifier is passed to AddressService.del(), whose failure response supplies the error object to this component's error callback.
The complete error object is emitted to the browser console rather than being reduced to a safe, non-sensitive diagnostic.

title: Login guard accepts an arbitrary token value as authentication
description: The authentication guard is tested as allowing access when localStorage contains the arbitrary string `TOKEN`; no valid JWT structure, signature verification, expiration check, or server-backed session validation is required in this exercised path. An attacker who can place any non-empty value in the browser's token storage could satisfy the login guard and reach routes protected only by it. This establishes an authentication failure and a resulting access-control bypass, although the guard implementation itself is in the imported `app.guard` file.

trace.description: The test supplies the guard's authentication state through browser localStorage. The caller and any attacker-controlled mechanism able to set this client-side value are outside this file.
The arbitrary value `TOKEN` is retained as the token input to the real `LoginGuard` instance obtained from Angular's test injector.

The guard returns `true` for the arbitrary token, demonstrating that this authentication gate can be passed without evidence of a valid, verified, or unexpired credential. This is the authentication and access-control sink.

title: Raw continue-code API errors are logged to the browser console
description: The component is expected to write errors returned by the continue-code API directly to the browser console. The test supplies an API error and verifies that the raw error value is passed to console.log. If the real API returns detailed errors containing account, token, or other sensitive context, this behavior exposes that information to anyone able to inspect the browser console and provides no structured security-event handling or redaction.

trace.description: The mocked continue-code API returns an error value to the component; the API implementation and attacker-facing caller are outside this test file.
The component's save-progress workflow processes the failed API call after being invoked by the test.
The test explicitly verifies that the raw error is written directly to console.log, establishing the browser-console logging sink without redaction or structured handling.

title: Unsanitized user email trusted as HTML
description: The component receives user records from the backend and replaces each email with a value produced by `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly disabling Angular's HTML sanitization. Because the email originates from an API response and may be attacker-controlled through a stored or otherwise modified user record, an attacker can supply HTML containing an XSS payload. If the component template renders this value through an HTML-binding context, the payload executes in other administrators' browsers.

trace.description: `findAllUsers` receives the `users` observable response from `UserService.find`; the caller and backend endpoint are outside this file.
Each returned user's `email` value is incorporated into a dynamically constructed HTML string containing a `<span>` element.

`DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml` marks the API-derived HTML as trusted and disables Angular's sanitization. Any attacker-controlled markup in `user.email` can therefore reach an HTML-rendering template binding and execute as client-side XSS.

title: Stored XSS in administrator feedback comments
description: The component receives feedback records from the backend and passes each feedback comment directly to `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, disabling Angular's built-in sanitization. A malicious user can submit a feedback comment containing executable HTML, which is then treated as trusted content when displayed in the administration interface. This creates stored client-side XSS against administrators or other users viewing the feedback list.

trace.description: `findAllFeedbacks` receives feedback data from `FeedbackService.find`; the caller and backend endpoint are outside this file.
The component iterates over every returned feedback record and takes its `comment` field without any visible validation or sanitization.

`feedback.comment` is passed directly to `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml`, explicitly marking attacker-supplied feedback content as safe HTML. When rendered by the component template, embedded HTML/script-capable payloads can execute in the viewer's browser.

title: Unbounded array allocation from caller-controlled count
description: The `times` method allocates an array whose length is directly determined by its caller, with no upper-bound or validity check. If an attacker-influenced value reaches this method, a very large positive value can cause excessive browser memory allocation and UI denial of service, while a negative or otherwise invalid value can trigger a runtime exception. The caller is outside this file, so the origin and reachability of `numberOfTimes` cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies the `numberOfTimes` argument to `times`. No bound or validation is enforced at this entrypoint.
The supplied count is passed directly into the JavaScript `Array` constructor without limiting its maximum size or rejecting invalid values.
`Array(numberOfTimes).fill('★')` allocates and initializes an array of the requested size, allowing an excessively large count to consume browser memory and potentially freeze or crash the page.

title: Unbounded processing of challenge-solved socket events
description: The component processes every incoming `challenge solved` socket event that contains a truthy `challenge`, without any visible rate limit, deduplication, event-count cap, or payload-size limit. Each accepted event can create a notification and, for non-restore events, dynamically load and execute the confetti effect. If an attacker can cause the server or an otherwise reachable Socket.IO channel to deliver repeated events, the browser can be driven into excessive DOM/UI work and repeated animation processing, degrading or freezing the victim's client.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the component registers a handler for externally received Socket.IO `challenge solved` messages; the socket and its server-side caller are outside this file.
The handler accepts any message with a truthy `data.challenge`; no rate, size, deduplication, or maximum-notification check is visible before processing it.
Each accepted non-hidden event is passed to `showNotification`, allowing repeated inbound events to trigger repeated notification work.
For every non-restore event, the handler dynamically imports the confetti module and invokes the animation effect. There is no throttling or coalescing of these expensive UI operations.

title: Raw country-mapping errors exposed through client console logging
description: A raw error object from the country-mapping request is written directly to the browser console. Browser-console output is visible to the user and may include backend error bodies, URLs, stack traces, or other implementation details depending on the HTTP client's error shape. This creates a low-severity information-exposure and incident-observability concern; the sensitivity of the actual error contents cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

trace.description: The component subscribes to application configuration received from outside this file and conditionally requests country-mapping data.
When country details are enabled, the component starts the country-mapping request and registers an error callback.
The raw error object is passed to `console.log`, exposing whatever diagnostic data the failed request provides in the user's browser console.

title: Unbounded growth of challenge notifications
description: The component accepts challenge-solved messages from a caller outside this file and appends one notification for every message without any maximum length, deduplication, expiration, or backpressure. An attacker who can cause repeated challenge-solved events, or an otherwise noisy/malicious event source, can grow the in-memory notification array and trigger repeated change detection, consuming browser memory and CPU and potentially degrading or freezing the client.

trace.description: `showNotification` receives a `ChallengeSolvedMessage` from a caller outside this file; this is the external data entrypoint for notification creation.
The message fields are copied into a notification object, including attacker-influenced challenge metadata such as `key`, `flag`, and `codingChallenge`.

Each received message is appended to `this.notifications` without a size limit or other resource control, followed by change detection. Repeated messages can therefore cause unbounded memory growth and repeated rendering work.

title: Address edit route lacks visible per-resource authorization control
description: The `address/edit/:addressId` route accepts a caller-controlled address identifier and protects the route only with `LoginGuard`, which establishes authentication but does not establish ownership or authorization for that specific address. A logged-in user can navigate directly to another user's address ID. If `AddressCreateComponent` or its backing API loads the address solely by `addressId` without a server-side ownership check, this becomes an IDOR/BOLA vulnerability. The required ownership enforcement is not visible in this routing file, so exploitability depends on downstream component/API behavior.

trace.description: Attacker-controlled navigation enters the Angular route with an arbitrary `addressId` path parameter; the caller is outside this file.
The route propagates the arbitrary `addressId` to `AddressCreateComponent`, while `LoginGuard` checks only whether the user is logged in.

`AddressCreateComponent` is made reachable for any authenticated user without a visible ownership/role guard tied to the selected address ID. Any downstream lookup or update using this ID must enforce ownership server-side.

title: Sensitive payment and order routes lack authentication guards
description: Sensitive account data is exposed through client routes that have no authentication guard. The file explicitly protects nearby account-related routes such as address creation and deluxe membership with LoginGuard, but saved-payment-methods, order-history, and wallet are directly routable without any canActivate control. An unauthenticated user can navigate to these components, which may cause sensitive payment, order, or wallet data to be loaded. Server-side API authorization cannot be confirmed from this file, so the finding is specifically the missing route-level access control and its resulting unauthenticated UI exposure.

trace.description: Attacker-controlled browser navigation enters the Angular route configuration; the caller is outside this file.
The router maps the unauthenticated navigation directly to SavedPaymentMethodsComponent, with no canActivate or equivalent authentication guard.
The same unguarded route block is followed by unguarded order-history and wallet routes, exposing sensitive account functionality to unauthenticated navigation.

title: Account security and data export routes are unguarded
description: The privacy and security settings area is reachable without an authentication guard, and its child routes include change-password, two-factor-authentication, and data-export operations. The parent route has no canActivate guard, and none of the shown children adds one. Consequently, an unauthenticated browser can directly navigate to account-security and data-export components. Whether the backing APIs independently enforce authentication is not visible here, but this routing configuration fails to enforce access control for these sensitive functions.

trace.description: An attacker navigates to the privacy-security route; the external browser request is received by Angular routing outside this file's route declaration logic.
PrivacySecurityComponent is registered without canActivate, so the parent route does not require an authenticated session before activating its children.
The child routes for change-password, two-factor-authentication, and data-export are also declared without guards; data-export is the final sensitive operation shown.

title: Identifier-bearing order and payment routes lack access and workflow gates
description: Routes accepting an order/resource identifier or payment entity are directly accessible without a LoginGuard: order-completion/:id and payment/:entity. The route configuration accepts attacker-selected values and activates the corresponding components without an authentication gate. If either component retrieves or mutates data based on the route parameter without independently enforcing ownership and workflow state, an attacker could substitute another order ID or entity and access or manipulate another user's transaction. The component/API checks are outside this file, so exploitability is not fully confirmed here.

trace.description: An attacker-controlled URL enters the Angular router with an arbitrary order id or payment entity; the caller is outside this file.
The router propagates the URL parameter into OrderCompletionComponent without canActivate or any visible prerequisite check.
PaymentComponent is likewise exposed through payment/:entity without a guard, leaving authorization, ownership, and payment-state validation to code not shown here.

title: Sensitive privacy and account-management routes lack visible authorization guards
description: The `privacy-security` route and its sensitive child routes are exposed without any route-level authorization guard (`canActivate`, role guard, or equivalent). A user can navigate directly to routes such as `privacy-security/change-password`, `data-export`, or `last-login-ip`, causing the corresponding components to be instantiated without an authorization decision in this routing configuration. If these components rely on routing as an access-control boundary, a user can bypass the intended workflow by entering the child URL directly; server-side API authorization is not visible in this file and would be required to prevent the bypass.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: a browser navigation or programmatic Angular navigation can enter the `privacy-security` route directly.
The route declares multiple security-sensitive child workflows but provides no `canActivate`, role, or prerequisite-state guard on the parent route.
The direct child route for changing the password is registered without an authorization or workflow guard, allowing direct navigation to the component.
The data-export and last-login-IP components are likewise directly routable without a visible authorization guard.

title: Obfuscated client-side route token is not an access-control boundary
description: The `tokenMatcher` uses a value reconstructed from constants embedded in the client bundle as the only condition for routing to `TokenSaleComponent`. Anyone who can download or inspect the frontend JavaScript can execute the same `token1`/`token2` logic, recover the accepted path string, and navigate directly to the supposedly token-gated route. A client-side, hardcoded obfuscation is not authentication or authorization. The impact depends on whether `TokenSaleComponent` exposes a privileged or otherwise restricted operation, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: an attacker-controlled browser URL supplies the first URL segment to Angular's custom matcher.
The matcher reads the caller-supplied segment and compares it against a value reconstructed entirely from constants shipped to the client.

The reconstructed token is used as the sole route-selection check; matching the discoverable value routes the attacker to `TokenSaleComponent`, with no server-side authorization or user/role check shown here.

title: Password-change handler submits invalid form values without enforcing validation
description: The component defines client-side validators for the password fields, but `changePassword()` never checks control validity before invoking the password-change service. An attacker can call the handler directly or trigger it through a crafted UI interaction with empty, too-short, too-long, or mismatched values, and those values are still submitted. If the backend relies on this client-side validation, the password-change workflow can be completed without satisfying its stated prerequisites.

trace.description: `changePassword()` is an externally callable component handler; its caller and template are outside this file.
The component declares required, length, and matching-password validators, establishing validation rules but not enforcement at the handler boundary.

title: Privileged password policy is advisory and based on client-controlled account identity

title: Payment method submission does not enforce form validity
description: `save()` constructs and submits a payment method without checking whether the form controls are valid. Although validators are attached to the controls, the method unconditionally reads their values and calls `paymentService.save`. Any caller that invokes `save()` outside the expected button state, or any UI path that fails to disable the button, can submit empty, malformed, or otherwise invalid card and expiry values. title: Authentication token persisted in JavaScript-accessible browser storage
description: The deluxe-payment flow persists the authentication token returned by the upgrade API in browser local storage and also writes it to a cookie. A bearer token in local storage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the origin, so an XSS or compromised third-party script can exfiltrate it and impersonate the user. The cookie write is also unsafe unless the underlying cookie service is verified to enforce Secure, SameSite, and preferably HttpOnly attributes; that control is not visible here. The test explicitly locks in this token-storage behavior, indicating it is part of the expected implementation.

The returned token is persisted under the authentication token key in Web Storage, making it directly readable by same-origin JavaScript.
The same bearer token is additionally written through the cookie service, whose security attributes are not established by this file.

title: Authentication state is based solely on a client-controlled localStorage token
description: The component's authentication state is treated as the mere presence and value of a client-controlled `localStorage` entry. The test stores the arbitrary string `abc` and expects `isLoggedIn()` to return it, then separately verifies that any stored value such as `token` causes the share-memory section and submit button to render. A user can create or modify this storage value locally without possessing a valid server-issued credential. This is not a server-side authorization bypass by itself, but it is an unsafe authentication design if this value is used as the security decision or forwarded as a bearer credential without independent server validation; at minimum, it allows unauthenticated users to unlock authenticated UI and can enable unauthorized requests if downstream code trusts the value.

The template behavior is exercised with an arbitrary localStorage value (`token`), rather than a demonstrably valid credential.

title: Unbounded client-side image read enables memory exhaustion
description: The component reads an arbitrarily large user-selected file into memory as a Base64 data URL and stores the expanded result in `imagePreview`. No size, dimension, or byte limit is enforced before `FileReader.readAsDataURL(file)` is invoked. A sufficiently large file can cause significant browser memory consumption, UI instability, or tab termination; the resulting file is also passed to the upload service without a size control visible in this file.

title: Unbounded photo-wall collection loading can exhaust client resources
description: On initialization, the component requests memories and assumes the response is the complete collection. It then iterates over every returned record and appends each one to an in-memory slideshow array. No pagination, result limit, cancellation, or client-side cap is applied. If the backing service returns an attacker-inflated or very large collection, a single page load can consume substantial client memory and rendering resources. title: Unbounded image file is read into memory and uploaded

No size limit or client-side resource guard is visible in this path. A user who selects a very large file can cause substantial browser memory consumption from both the FileReader result and upload buffering; if the backend also lacks independent upload limits, the same request can consume server memory, bandwidth, and storage. A FileReader is created and instructed to read the entire attacker-selected file as a data URL, allocating memory proportional to the full file size and adding base64 expansion.

The complete data URL is retained in imagePreview, while the original file is submitted to the upload service. A sufficiently large local file can therefore create excessive client memory use and an unbounded upload request if downstream limits are absent.

title: Client-controlled payment amount submitted to wallet service
description: The payment amount is derived from browser-controlled sessionStorage and then submitted to the wallet service as the payment balance. In wallet mode, `walletTotal` is read directly without server-side re-derivation or validation in this component, and `choosePayment()` sends the resulting `totalPrice` to `walletService.put()`. An attacker can modify `sessionStorage.walletTotal` before reaching this flow and submit an arbitrarily low, zero, negative, or otherwise manipulated balance, potentially obtaining wallet credit or completing a purchase for an incorrect amount if the backend trusts the supplied balance. The same design also uses client-controlled `itemTotal` and `couponDiscount` when calculating non-wallet totals.

A token in localStorage is readable by any JavaScript executing in the origin, so an XSS or compromised third-party script can extract it and impersonate the user. description: The component constructs a review request with an identity assertion supplied by the browser: `author` is a public mutable property and is placed directly into the request body. title: Client-controlled basket ID enables potential cross-user basket access
description: The component uses a client-controlled session-storage value as the basket identifier for an authenticated basket lookup. A user can modify `sessionStorage.bid` in browser developer tools and cause the component to request another basket ID. This file performs no ownership or authorization check before assigning the returned basket to `dataSource`; exploitation depends on whether the backend service enforces ownership, which is not visible here.

The client-controlled identifier is passed to `BasketService.find`, and the returned basket is accepted and rendered without any per-resource authorization check in this component. An attacker can replace `bid` with another user's basket ID and attempt to retrieve that basket.

title: Unbounded guest basket fan-out creates excessive product requests
description: Guest basket contents are read from client-side storage and every stored item is converted into an independent product request. There is no item-count, request-count, or other workload cap before `forkJoin` subscribes to all requests simultaneously. An attacker can populate or repeatedly manipulate their guest basket with many entries, causing a burst of outbound product requests and corresponding browser/server work. The ultimate impact depends on limits enforced by `BasketService`, the API, or infrastructure outside this file.

title: Guest basket quantities can become zero or negative
description: The guest-basket quantity path does not enforce a minimum quantity. `dec()` passes `-1` to `addToQuantity()`, and the guest branch persists `existingGuestItem.quantity + value` without the lower-bound clamp used by the authenticated branch. A guest can therefore reduce an item from quantity 1 to 0 or negative values. When the basket is reloaded, those values flow into the client-side total and bonus calculations, producing negative or otherwise invalid purchase amounts. If these client-calculated values are used by checkout or trusted by downstream code, this enables price/loyalty manipulation; even if the server later rejects it, the component exposes an inconsistent business state.

The unchecked quantity is written back to the guest basket, allowing zero or negative quantities to persist in client state.

After reloading, the persisted quantity is multiplied into the item total and bonus calculation. Negative quantities consequently produce negative totals or bonus values that are emitted to the parent component.

title: Client-side-only recycling quantity limits can be bypassed
description: The recycling quantity constraint is enforced only by Angular form validators, while the value is copied directly into the request object and submitted. A caller can bypass the browser UI or alter the request and submit a quantity below 10, above 1000, or a non-numeric value. The server-side enforcement cannot be confirmed from this file, but this component provides no server-independent protection for the business rule.

The resulting object is submitted through the recycling service. A modified client or direct HTTP request can supply an arbitrarily small, large, or otherwise invalid quantity; if the API does not independently enforce the same bounds, this can violate recycling business rules and potentially increase processing/resource consumption.

title: Client-controlled UserId is submitted as an authorization-relevant property
description: The component places the authenticated user's identifier into a mutable, untyped request object and sends that object to the recycle API. Because the identifier is a client-supplied request property, a caller can alter UserId before submission or replace the request entirely. If the backend authorizes the recycle record based on this property rather than deriving the user from the authenticated session, this enables creating a recycle request attributed to another user. Server-side ownership enforcement is not visible in this file.

The mutable recycle object, including UserId, is sent to the recycle service. An attacker can change UserId in the browser or network request; if accepted by the API without deriving identity from authentication and checking ownership, the request can be attributed to another account.

description: The component retrieves the complete recycle collection through `recycleService.find()` without any visible pagination, result cap, or client-side limit. If the backing `GET /api/Recycles` endpoint returns an unbounded collection, an attacker or repeatedly invoked client can force large response bodies and browser memory consumption, while the server must also load and serialize the full collection for each request. title: Raw error objects written to client logs

title: Client-controlled basket ID used for authenticated basket access
description: The component treats the basket identifier in browser-controlled sessionStorage as the target for authenticated basket operations. A caller can alter the `bid` value before invoking this component, causing `basketService.find()` and subsequent `basketService.put()` calls to operate on an arbitrary basket. This component performs no ownership or authorization check tying the basket to the current user; if the backend endpoint does not independently enforce ownership, User A can substitute User B's basket ID, read its contents, and increment its items. The `isLoggedIn` input is also only a client-side branch control and is not an authorization mechanism.

For the authenticated branch, the component reads `bid` directly from browser-controlled sessionStorage and converts it into the basket identifier. No server-derived or user-bound basket reference is established here.

After locating an item in the selected basket, the component updates that basket item using its ID and a newly calculated quantity, again without an ownership check. If the service/API accepts the arbitrary basket, an attacker can modify another user's basket.

title: Client-controlled basket identifier enables cross-basket mutation

An attacker can modify the `bid` value in browser storage before invoking the add-to-cart flow, causing the request to target a different basket. This becomes a broken object-level authorization vulnerability if the backend accepts the supplied BasketId without deriving the basket from the authenticated session and verifying ownership. The payload is sent to the basket service without any per-basket ownership or authorization check in this component. If the API trusts the submitted BasketId, changing `sessionStorage.bid` to another user's basket identifier lets an attacker add products to that basket, corrupting its contents or potentially affecting another user's order.

description: The registration form explicitly accepts passwords as short as five characters (`Validators.minLength(5)`). If the backend relies on this client-side validation or does not enforce a stronger policy, attackers can create accounts with low-entropy passwords that are substantially easier to brute-force or guess. The `save()` method submits the control values directly to the registration service, and it does not perform any stronger password-policy check in this file. title: Client-controlled hint unlock state

If the backend accepts this field as authoritative, an attacker can invoke the client method or reproduce the request to unlock hints without satisfying the intended challenge, payment, or entitlement requirements. title: Wallet transactions are not restricted to an approved blockchain network
description: The component reacts to wallet chain changes by re-running authentication, but never verifies that the connected chain is an approved/expected network before allowing deposits or withdrawals. The injected provider used for the transaction is the wallet's currently selected network, while the bank contract address is only a hardcoded address and is not accompanied by a chain-ID check. A user can connect or switch to an unsupported network where the same address contains a different contract or no trusted contract, then approve a transaction believing it targets the intended bank. description: The component submits the connected wallet address to the backend as soon as the wallet connection succeeds, but performs no challenge/response signature or other cryptographic proof that the caller controls that address. This is the authentication/business-logic sink: possession of a claimed address is treated as sufficient input without proof of control.

title: Plaintext user password embedded in frontend source
description: The frontend challenge instruction embeds Bender's plaintext password in client-side source. Because this exported instruction object is part of the frontend bundle, any user can inspect the JavaScript and recover the credential, then authenticate directly as Bender. The value is used as a known-password check by the challenge helper, but that does not prevent it from being shipped to the client.

The challenge config passes the plaintext string `OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!` as the password value to reject while waiting for user input.
The plaintext password is embedded directly in the shipped frontend source/configuration, allowing any client who can load the challenge bundle to recover it and use it for Bender authentication.

title: Plaintext account credential embedded in frontend source
description: The frontend challenge source contains Jim's apparent plaintext password, `ncc-1701`, in a client-delivered instruction/helper call. Because frontend source is available to users, anyone who can access this challenge can retrieve the credential without authentication and attempt direct login as Jim. If this is only isolated training-fixture data, the impact is limited to that fixture account; otherwise it is a credential-disclosure issue.

The challenge explicitly directs the user to enter an arbitrary password, while the helper invocation includes a known password value used to distinguish the real password from the supplied value.
The plaintext value `ncc-1701`, which is presented as Jim's possible existing password, is hardcoded in source shipped to the frontend.

title: Mint function exposed without visible authorization evidence
description: The public ABI exposes a nonpayable `mintTokens(recipient, amount)` operation that can be invoked by any caller able to submit a transaction. This file contains no evidence of caller authorization or role enforcement before token creation. If the underlying contract does not enforce an owner/minter restriction, an attacker could mint arbitrary tokens to any address; authorization cannot be confirmed from this ABI alone.

trace.description: Caller outside this file can use the exported contract ABI to construct and submit a transaction invoking the contract's mint operation.
The ABI accepts caller-supplied `recipient` and `amount` values, including an arbitrary destination and token quantity.

`mintTokens` is declared as a nonpayable contract function with no authorization requirement represented in this ABI. Any real protection must exist in the underlying contract implementation, which is not shown here.

title: Token minting operation exposed without visible authorization control
description: The ABI exposes a nonpayable `mintTokens(address recipient, uint256 amount)` operation that accepts an arbitrary recipient and amount, with no authorization information or restriction represented in this file. If the underlying token contract does not enforce an owner/minter check, any caller able to use this frontend contract interface can mint tokens to any address, creating unbacked supply and potentially bypassing the application's intended economic controls. The implementation and caller are outside this file, so reachability and the presence of an on-chain authorization guard cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: Caller and transaction entrypoint are outside this file; an external caller can use the contract interface represented by this ABI to invoke the declared token function.
The operation accepts caller-supplied `recipient` and `amount` values, allowing the caller to choose both the beneficiary and quantity of newly minted tokens.

The ABI declares `mintTokens` as a nonpayable state-changing function and shows no access-control constraint. An on-chain implementation that omits authorization would permit arbitrary token creation.

title: Unsanitized markdown inserted with innerHTML
description: The instructor renders `snarkdown(hint.text)` directly through `innerHTML`. Markdown parsers commonly preserve or generate raw HTML, and no sanitizer or safe DOM-text rendering is applied before insertion. `startHackingInstructorFor` is exported and receives its challenge name from a caller outside this file; it selects the hint content that reaches this sink. If any hint text is attacker-influenced through challenge data, deployment customization, or another caller-controlled source, an attacker can supply HTML such as an event-handler payload and execute script in the application's origin. The shown code does not establish that `hint.text` is externally controlled, so exploitability is not fully confirmable from this chunk.

trace.description: `startHackingInstructorFor` is an exported entrypoint receiving `challengeName`; its caller is outside this file.
The function selects a challenge instruction and iterates over its hint objects; the selected hint's `text` is passed to `loadHint`.
`loadHint` converts `hint.text` with `snarkdown` and assigns the result directly to `textBox.innerHTML`, with no visible sanitization or allowlist between the content and the DOM sink.

title: Unbounded client-side polling can consume browser resources
description: The exported wait helpers implement unbounded polling with no timeout, cancellation mechanism, or maximum retry count. A caller outside this file can provide an input selector/value combination that never becomes satisfied, causing the returned asynchronous function to remain alive indefinitely and wake every 100 ms. Repeated invocation can accumulate persistent timers and consume browser event-loop resources, degrading or freezing the client tab. This is primarily a client-side resource-consumption weakness; exploitability depends on whether an attacker can influence invocation or cause many waits to be registered.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and receives an exported wait-helper factory. The caller controls the input selector and expected value passed to the helper.
The helper obtains a DOM element from the caller-provided selector and enters an unconditional loop that only exits when the element value matches the requested value.

When the condition never becomes true, the loop repeatedly schedules another wake-up every 100 ms forever. The same unbounded pattern is also present in the related wait helpers at lines 71, 88, and 107, allowing persistent polling tasks to accumulate.

title: Unbounded DOM polling can accumulate indefinitely
description: Several exported helpers poll indefinitely until a DOM condition becomes true, with no timeout, cancellation mechanism, or maximum retry count. In particular, a caller outside this file can invoke this helper with a selector that never matches or whose content never equals the supplied value. The unresolved promise and recurring 100 ms timers remain active indefinitely; repeated invocations can accumulate pending polling loops and consume browser CPU and memory, degrading the client or hanging an instructor workflow.

trace.description: Entrypoint: a caller outside this file invokes the exported waitForElementsInnerHtmlToBe helper with an element selector and expected value.
The returned asynchronous function enters an unconditional while(true) loop and repeatedly queries the DOM for the requested element.
If the element is absent or its innerHTML never matches, the loop sleeps for 100 ms and retries forever, with no timeout or cancellation control.

title: Admin state is inferred from an unverified client-side JWT payload
description: The admin-login helper treats a locally stored JWT's decoded payload as authoritative for determining whether the client is in an admin state. jwtDecode only parses the token; it does not verify the JWT signature, issuer, audience, or expiration. An attacker who can write or replace the localStorage token can place a token containing data.role = 'admin', causing this helper to pass the admin gate even though the token is not authentic. This file does not show a protected server-side operation, so the impact depends on callers relying on this client-side gate; server-side authorization would be required to prevent privilege escalation.

trace.description: Entrypoint: a caller outside this file invokes the exported waitForAdminLogIn helper, which is intended to wait until the client appears to be logged in as an administrator.
The helper obtains the token directly from browser-controlled localStorage.
The token is decoded locally with jwtDecode and the payload is read without any signature, issuer, audience, or expiration verification.
The decoded payload's data.role value is copied into the role variable and is then trusted as the authorization state.
The helper exits successfully solely when the unverified, client-controlled role equals 'admin'.

title: Unbounded client-side Solidity compilation enables resource exhaustion
description: The component accepts an externally supplied Solidity source string and passes it directly to the Solidity compiler without any size, complexity, or execution-frequency limit. Compilation is an expensive CPU and memory operation, and compiler diagnostics are appended to a persistent array. A caller can repeatedly submit very large or deliberately compiler-intensive contracts, causing browser CPU exhaustion and potentially unbounded growth of `compilerErrors`, degrading or freezing the client.

trace.description: `compileAndFetchContracts(code)` receives the contract source from a caller outside this file; this is the attacker-controlled entrypoint for compilation input.
The supplied `code` is placed directly into `compilerInput.contractBody` without a maximum length or complexity check.

The unbounded input is passed to `solidityCompiler`, an expensive compilation operation. Compilation errors are also appended to `compilerErrors` without a bound, allowing repeated requests to consume additional client memory.

title: Unbounded contract argument parsing can consume browser resources
description: The wallet-connected UI accepts an arbitrary-length comma-separated argument string and expands it with `split(',').map(...)` before invoking a contract function. There is no input-size, argument-count, or per-call resource bound in this component. An attacker or automated caller that can supply a very large `func.inputValues` value can force substantial browser memory allocation and parsing work, and can repeatedly trigger contract calls through the same path. The contract/provider may reject malformed arguments, but the unbounded client-side parsing and call construction remains a denial-of-service risk. The caller of `invokeFunction` is outside this file.

trace.description: `invokeFunction(func)` receives the function descriptor, including `func.inputValues`, from a caller outside this file. The only gate shown is whether `this.session` is truthy; no size or invocation-rate limit is enforced.

The entire trimmed input string is split into an unbounded array and each element is mapped and parsed. A sufficiently large attacker-controlled string therefore causes proportional memory allocation and CPU work before the blockchain call is attempted.

The expanded argument array is spread into a contract function invocation using the connected signer. Repeated or oversized calls can consume browser resources and initiate repeated provider/wallet work without an application-level bound.

title: Client session state is derived from network selection without wallet authentication
description: The component marks the user as having an active session solely after observing that the connected provider reports the Sepolia chain ID. No wallet signature, account-ownership proof, token validation, or server-side authentication result is established in this code. If downstream functionality treats `this.session` as an authenticated session, an attacker can set or simulate the client-side connection state and obtain an authenticated UI state without proving control of the wallet account. The impact depends on whether this flag gates security-sensitive operations elsewhere.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; provider-derived account and chain data are received and used to construct the wallet/network state at this component location.

The component converts the provider-reported chain identifier into a string and compares it with the expected Sepolia chain ID. This verifies only network selection, not ownership of the reported account or authenticity of an authenticated session.

When the chain ID matches, the component sets `this.session = true` without a signature challenge, token verification, or other authentication check. Any security-sensitive behavior relying on this client-side flag could therefore be reached without wallet authentication.

title: Unbounded recursive filesystem scanning enables resource exhaustion
description: The exported `findFilesWithCodeChallenges` function accepts caller-supplied filesystem paths and recursively traverses every directory and reads every encountered file without depth, file-count, or file-size limits. If reachable from an attacker-influenced caller, a path targeting a large directory tree, recursively expanding symlink structure, or very large files can consume substantial filesystem I/O, memory, and CPU and degrade availability.

trace.description: `findFilesWithCodeChallenges` is an exported entrypoint; its `paths` argument is supplied by a caller outside this file and is not constrained to the intended repository paths.
Each caller-provided path is inspected and directories are recursively enumerated; there is no traversal depth, entry-count, or total-work limit.
Directory contents are converted into absolute paths and passed back into the same recursive function, allowing unbounded traversal of the supplied tree.
Every non-directory path encountered is read in full as UTF-8, with no file-size or aggregate byte limit.

title: Unescaped filesystem-derived challenge keys are used as dynamic regular expressions
description: Challenge identifiers are extracted from filesystem file contents and interpolated directly into dynamically constructed regular expressions. The identifier is not escaped or allow-listed. A file containing regex metacharacters can alter the matching expression, trigger a `RegExp` construction exception, or create expensive backtracking against a large source string. Because the challenge files are read from the filesystem and the caller of `getCodeChallenges` is outside this file, exploitability depends on whether an attacker can influence files in the scanned paths, but the unsafe dynamic-regex construction is present.

trace.description: `getCodeChallenges` is an exported entrypoint invoked by a caller outside this file; it initializes challenge discovery using repository paths.
The function scans files under the configured paths and passes each file's raw content to challenge parsing.
Challenge keys are parsed from the file content and passed into `getCodingChallengeFromFileContent` without a character allow-list or regex escaping.
The raw `challengeKey` is interpolated into a `String.match` pattern, causing it to be interpreted as regular-expression syntax rather than treated as literal data.

title: Challenge flags broadcast to all connected clients
description: The notification object includes the challenge flag and is broadcast through the global Socket.IO instance to every connected client. A caller outside this file invokes the exported notification path after a challenge is solved, and the code does not scope delivery to the solver or verify that recipients are authorized to receive the flag. Any connected user may therefore learn a challenge flag when another user solves it, undermining challenge secrecy and enabling unauthorized solution disclosure.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file and supplies a ChallengeModel to the exported sendNotification function.
The function derives the challenge flag from the challenge name and places it into the notification data.
The notification object explicitly contains the derived flag along with other challenge data.
The notification, including the flag, is emitted on the global Socket.IO instance without recipient- or authorization-based filtering.

title: Unbounded growth of in-memory challenge notifications
description: Every solved challenge notification is appended to the shared notifications array, but the array is never bounded, pruned, or deduplicated. The duplicate check only controls whether a non-restore event is emitted; it does not prevent notifications.push. Repeated calls to the exported solve/sendNotification path—especially with isRestore=true, which permits repeated emissions—can cause unbounded in-memory growth and, for connected clients, repeated network work, eventually degrading or exhausting server resources.

trace.description: A caller outside this file can invoke the exported solve function, which accepts a challenge and an isRestore flag and subsequently invokes sendNotification.
solve passes the challenge and restore state into sendNotification after saving it as solved.
sendNotification computes whether an equivalent notification was previously shown, but this value only controls emission conditions and does not constrain storage.
The notification is appended unconditionally to the shared notifications array, allowing repeated calls to grow it without limit.

title: Unconditional transition allows skipping the Find It phase
description: The exported solveFixIt helper transitions a challenge directly to codingChallengeStatus 2 without verifying that the challenge is currently in the preceding Find It state. A caller outside this file that can invoke the helper can skip the required workflow step and mark a challenge as fixed/completed directly. Unlike solveFindIt, which constrains the update with codingChallengeStatus < 2, this update has only a key predicate.

trace.description: Exported solveFixIt receives the challenge key and restore flag; its caller is outside this file, so any authorization or workflow guarantees from the caller are not enforced here.
The helper resolves the challenge from the caller-supplied key but performs no check that the challenge is in the expected prior state before proceeding.

ChallengeModel.update sets codingChallengeStatus to 2 using only the key predicate. There is no condition requiring the prior Find It status, allowing a direct state transition that skips the required phase.

title: Google OAuth redirect destinations are unrestricted
description: The exported application configuration schema accepts Google OAuth redirect destinations as arbitrary strings. `authorizedRedirects[].uri` and the optional `proxy` field are not constrained to approved HTTPS origins, same-site URLs, or another safe redirect-URI policy. If configuration is attacker-influenced through a writable deployment/configuration path, an attacker can add an external callback destination and potentially cause OAuth authorization responses to be redirected to an attacker-controlled host, enabling credential or authorization-code interception depending on downstream OAuth handling. The schema itself provides no control against this dangerous configuration.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies application configuration that is validated using the exported `ApplicationSchema`.
The application schema includes the Google OAuth configuration section, causing the externally supplied OAuth settings to be accepted through this schema.

`authorizedRedirects` accepts any string for `uri`, and `proxy` also accepts any string without origin, scheme, host, or allowlist validation. A downstream OAuth configuration or redirect handler can therefore receive attacker-controlled redirect destinations if the configuration source is compromised or writable.

title: Product economics are not constrained to non-negative values
description: The product configuration accepts economically meaningful numeric values without enforcing business invariants. `price`, `deluxePrice`, `limitPerUser`, and `quantity` are validated only as generic numbers, so negative values are accepted; the deep-partial validation path also permits incomplete product objects. If an attacker can supply or influence a YAML configuration consumed by this schema, they can configure products with negative prices or quantities, potentially creating credits, reversing charges, bypassing purchase limits, or otherwise corrupting product economics. The downstream business logic is outside this file, but the schema does not establish the required non-negative bounds.

trace.description: The exported validation schema receives possibly attacker-influenced YAML configuration data; the caller and YAML upload path are outside this file.
The `products` collection is validated using `ProductSchema.partial()`, so custom configuration entries may omit fields while retaining the weak numeric validation from the product schema.

The product price is accepted as any Zod number with no non-negative or other business-limit constraint. The same pattern is present for `deluxePrice`, `limitPerUser`, and `quantity` at lines 130-137.

title: Unescaped application name enables stored HTML/script injection
description: The configured application name is inserted directly into the generated frontend HTML without HTML escaping. If an attacker can influence the application configuration (for example through a configuration-management compromise or writable deployment settings), a value such as `</title><script>...</script>` is written into `index.html` and executed by every user loading the application. The caller and configuration source are outside this file, so reachability of attacker-controlled configuration cannot be confirmed here.

The application name is read from configuration and interpolated into a `<title>` element without HTML escaping.
The resulting attacker-influenced string is supplied as the replacement text to `replace`, which writes it into the served `frontend/dist/frontend/index.html`.

title: Unescaped cookie-consent configuration allows frontend injection
description: Cookie-consent configuration values are concatenated into an HTML/JSON-like fragment and written into the public frontend without escaping or safe serialization. A malicious message, label, link text, or URL can break out of quoted values and inject markup or script; additionally, a `javascript:` link URL may be emitted directly into the generated `href`. The configuration caller is outside this file, so exploitation depends on an attacker obtaining control over these configuration values.
