Cookie-consent message, dismissal text, link text, and link URL are concatenated into quoted markup without HTML escaping, JSON serialization, or URL-scheme validation.
The resulting fragment is used as replacement text for content in the public `index.html`, allowing configuration-controlled markup or script content to reach clients.

title: Theme configuration is inserted into HTML without escaping
description: The configured theme name is inserted into a quoted HTML attribute by string concatenation. A value containing quotes and attribute syntax can terminate the intended class value and add attacker-controlled attributes or markup when the generated index is served. The configuration source is outside this file, so the attacker’s ability to modify it is not established.

trace.description: `customizeApplication` is invoked by a caller outside this file and applies the configured theme during startup.
The theme value is concatenated between quotes with a `-theme` suffix, with no validation or HTML attribute escaping.
The constructed value is written into the public frontend HTML through the `replace` call, where embedded quotes and attributes can become active markup.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key enables JWT forgery
description: The application embeds an RSA private key directly in source code and uses it to sign authentication tokens. Anyone who obtains the source or compiled artifact can recover the private key and create valid RS256 JWTs for arbitrary users, roles, or claims. The resulting forged tokens will be accepted by middleware configured with the corresponding public key.

trace.description: The exported authorize function receives caller-supplied token claims through its user parameter; the caller is outside this file.
The token is signed with RS256 and the module-level privateKey value rather than a protected runtime secret or key-management system.
The privateKey is hardcoded in the source file, including RSA private key material, so an attacker who obtains the source or artifact can sign arbitrary authentication tokens.

title: Hardcoded HMAC secret permits forgery of authenticated data
description: The HMAC helper uses a hardcoded, reusable secret. Exposure of this source reveals the key and allows attackers to generate valid HMAC values for any data protected with this helper, defeating integrity or authentication checks that rely on it.

trace.description: The exported hmac function receives arbitrary data from callers outside this file.
The supplied data is processed using HMAC-SHA256 with a fixed literal key shared by every invocation.
The literal HMAC key is embedded in source code, allowing anyone with source or artifact access to reproduce valid MACs and forge protected values.

title: Exported MD5 helper is unsuitable for authentication secrets
description: The exported hash helper computes an unsalted MD5 digest with no key stretching. If used for passwords, reset values, or other authentication material by callers outside this file, attackers can efficiently brute-force or use precomputed tables against the resulting values. The function provides no password-specific protection such as bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2.

trace.description: The exported hash function receives data from callers outside this file; the file does not constrain that data to non-sensitive values.
The data is hashed directly with MD5 and no salt, work factor, or password-specific key derivation is applied.
The MD5 digest is returned as the security-relevant result, creating a weak storage or verification primitive when callers use it for credentials or authentication tokens.

title: Unsigned coupons can be forged for arbitrary discounts
description: Coupon validation checks only that a coupon decodes to the current month and a two-digit discount. There is no signature, MAC, server-side lookup, or other authenticity check. An attacker can construct a Z85-encoded value such as the current MMMYY followed by '-99' and have it accepted as a valid high-discount coupon.

trace.description: The exported discountFromCoupon function receives a coupon value from a caller outside this file, such as an HTTP request handler.
The caller-controlled value is decoded from Z85 and accepted when it matches the current-month format; Z85 is only an encoding and does not authenticate the value.

The decoded discount component is parsed and returned without any cryptographic authenticity check or server-side validation, so an attacker-generated current-month coupon can obtain the encoded discount.

title: User identity is trusted from a spoofable request header
description: The helper derives an email identity directly from the x-user-email request header. HTTP headers are caller-controlled unless a trusted upstream component strips and rewrites them, and this function performs no verification against a signed token or authenticated session. Any caller using this helper for identity or authorization can therefore be impersonated by supplying another user's email.

trace.description: The exported userEmailFrom helper receives the request headers object from a caller outside this file.
It selects x-user-email directly from the incoming headers without consulting the authenticated JWT, session, or a server-side user record.
The unverified header value is returned as the user's email and can be consumed by callers as an identity or authorization decision, enabling impersonation when the header is client-controlled.

title: Coupons lack integrity protection and can be forged
description: The coupon value is only Z85-encoded, not authenticated or signed. An attacker who can submit a coupon can construct an encoded value containing the current month/year and an arbitrary two-digit discount, such as `MMMYY-99`; `discountFromCoupon` decodes it, checks only the format and month, and returns the attacker-selected discount. This permits unauthorized discount creation and undermines coupon integrity.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies the attacker-controlled coupon string to the exported `discountFromCoupon` function.
The supplied coupon is reversibly decoded with Z85; this provides encoding only and does not verify that the coupon was issued by the server.
The decoded value is accepted when it contains a month/year and two digits matching the expected format, without any signature, MAC, or lookup against issued coupons.
The current-month check is followed by parsing and returning the caller-controlled discount component, allowing a forged coupon to grant an arbitrary two-digit discount.
The attacker-controlled discount is returned as the effective discount value.

title: Redirect allowlist is bypassable through substring matching
description: `isRedirectAllowed` attempts to enforce a destination allowlist using substring matching. A URL is accepted if it merely contains an allowed URL, so an attacker can append attacker-controlled content or use a lookalike destination containing an allowlisted string, for example `https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop.attacker.example`. If the caller uses this predicate to authorize redirects, the allowlist can be bypassed and users can be redirected to an untrusted site.

trace.description: The caller outside this file supplies a candidate redirect URL to the exported `isRedirectAllowed` function.
The function iterates over the configured trusted redirect destinations.
It authorizes the candidate URL when it contains an allowlisted URL anywhere, rather than requiring an exact URL or validating the origin and path structurally.

title: Authentication token cookie lacks secure session attributes
description: The middleware places a JWT into a response cookie without specifying security attributes. Express therefore does not add `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, or `SameSite` based on this call. The token can be exposed to client-side script through XSS, sent over an unencrypted HTTP connection, and may be sent in cross-site requests, increasing the impact of token theft and CSRF. The issue is especially relevant because this middleware accepts the token from either a cookie or request-derived token and persists it for subsequent authentication.

trace.description: The exported middleware receives an HTTP request and response from the application framework; the route caller is outside this file.
The middleware obtains the authentication token from a cookie or request-derived token and verifies it before caching it.
After successful JWT verification, the middleware persists the token in the authenticated-user map and writes it back to the client as a cookie.

The token cookie is set without `httpOnly`, `secure`, or `sameSite` options, leaving it readable by JavaScript and usable over insecure transport or cross-site requests depending on deployment and browser defaults.

title: Unvalidated domain enables server-side request forgery
description: The exported `checkIfDomainReachable` function accepts an arbitrary caller-provided `domain` and passes it directly to `fetch` without restricting the scheme, hostname, IP range, or redirect destination. If an attacker can reach a caller of this exported function, they can cause the server to make requests to internal services such as loopback addresses, private-network hosts, or cloud metadata endpoints. The five-second timeout limits request duration but does not prevent SSRF.

trace.description: `checkIfDomainReachable` is an exported entrypoint receiving `domain`; its caller is outside this file and may supply attacker-controlled data.
The supplied `domain` is propagated directly into the outbound request options and is not subject to an allowlist or private-address validation.
`fetch(domain, ...)` performs the server-side network request to the caller-selected destination.

title: Caller-controlled port enables local service probing
description: The exported `checkIfPortIsAvailable` function accepts a caller-controlled port and passes the parsed value to `portscanner.checkPortStatus`. The port scanner's two-argument form commonly probes the local host by default, allowing a reachable caller to test whether services are listening on arbitrary local ports. This can expose internal service availability and provide a limited internal network-probing primitive. The finding depends on whether an attacker can reach a caller of this startup helper.

trace.description: `checkIfPortIsAvailable` is an exported entrypoint receiving a caller-controlled `port`; its caller is outside this file.
The input is converted with `parseInt` but is otherwise not restricted to an approved port or protected from repeated probing.
The resulting port is passed to `portscanner.checkPortStatus`, which initiates a network connectivity check, typically against the scanner's default local host when no host is supplied.

title: Unvalidated LLM API URL enables server-side request forgery
description: The exported `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` function accepts an arbitrary `llmApiUrl` from callers outside this file and interpolates it directly into a server-side `fetch` request. No allowlist, scheme restriction, hostname validation, or private-address blocking is applied. The nearby `isOllamaUrl` helper only classifies the URL for a log message and is not used to constrain the request destination. If an attacker can influence the caller-supplied URL or the configuration passed to this function, the server can be induced to request internal services such as localhost administration endpoints or cloud metadata services, potentially exposing the response through observable application behavior or causing internal side effects.

trace.description: `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` is an exported entrypoint receiving `llmApiUrl`; its caller is outside this file. The parameter determines the destination of a subsequent server-side network request.

The caller-provided URL is directly interpolated into the request target with no visible allowlist or private-network protection. The five-second timeout limits duration but does not restrict the destination.

title: Missing ownership check when updating basket items
description: The PUT basket-item authorization middleware looks up the requested basket item by its caller-controlled ID but never verifies that the item belongs to the authenticated user's basket. The authenticated user is retrieved at line 68 but is unused. For requests that do not provide a quantity, the handler immediately calls next(), and for quantity updates it only validates product stock before allowing the downstream update. User A can submit User B's basket-item ID and modify its quantity.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler is used for PUT /api/BasketItems/:id; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The target basket-item identifier enters through req.params.id.
The caller-controlled ID is used in an unscoped database lookup, with no BasketId or user ownership predicate.
The handler obtains the authenticated user, but does not compare that user's basket ID with the retrieved item's BasketId.
The handler calls next() without an ownership decision, allowing the downstream PUT operation to update the item identified by another user's ID.

title: Basket ID authorization validates a different value than the one persisted
description: The POST handler collects every supplied BasketId, checks only basketIds[0] against the authenticated user's basket, but persists basketIds[basketIds.length - 1]. An authenticated attacker can provide a first BasketId belonging to their own basket so the authorization check succeeds, followed by a second BasketId belonging to another user's basket. The final value is then saved, allowing insertion into another user's basket.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported handler is used for POST /api/BasketItems; the caller and route registration are outside this file. The request body is received as rawBody.
The raw request body is parsed into key/value entries controlled by the caller.
All supplied BasketId values are accumulated rather than rejecting duplicate BasketId fields.
Authorization checks only the first supplied BasketId against the authenticated user's basket.
The basket item is constructed using the last supplied BasketId, which may differ from the value that passed authorization.
The attacker-controlled item, including the unauthorized final BasketId, is persisted by save().

title: Negative basket quantities bypass stock and per-user limits
description: The quantity validation accepts negative quantities. For a negative quantity, product.limitPerUser >= quantity and product.quantity >= quantity are both true, so the request proceeds. The negative value is then copied into the BasketItem model and saved. This permits creation of invalid cart state and can produce business-logic manipulation when basket totals or stock calculations process the item.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the exported POST handler receives caller-controlled basket-item data; the route caller is outside this file.
The quantity field from the parsed request is collected without a positivity or non-negative constraint.
The route's quantity-check middleware forwards the request quantity into quantityCheck.
The quantity is used in the business-rule checks without first rejecting values below zero.
A negative quantity satisfies the per-user limit comparison, because the limit is greater than or equal to the negative value.
A negative quantity also satisfies the stock comparison, because available stock is greater than or equal to the negative value; next() therefore permits the add operation.
The unchecked negative quantity is copied into the basket-item object.

title: Mass assignment permits caller-controlled role and account status
